paragraphs.heading: The shape in numbers
paragraphs.text: A shield volcano is named for its low profile, which looks like a shield lying on the ground. Its slope is gentle, usually 2° to 3°. The slope gradually steepens with elevation, reaching about 10°, and then flattens near the summit. In height, shield volcanoes are typically about one twentieth of their width.

paragraphs.heading: Thin sheets of runny lava
paragraphs.text: The form comes from the lava. Hawaiian eruptions, the kind typical of shield volcanoes, give out highly fluid basaltic lavas with low gas content. These lavas travel much farther than those of other eruptive types before they harden. They form sheets that are extremely wide but relatively thin, often less than 1 m thick. Small volumes of such lava, laid down in layers over long periods, slowly build the low, broad profile of a mature shield volcano.

paragraphs.heading: How shields differ from other types
paragraphs.text: Shield volcanoes are set apart from the three other major types of volcano, which are stratovolcanoes, lava domes and cinder cones. Of the four, shield volcanoes erupt the least viscous lavas. Stratovolcanoes and lava domes come from highly viscous flows. Cinder cones are built of tephra from explosive eruptions. Shield volcanoes are the product of gentle effusive eruptions.

paragraphs.heading: Hawaiian eruptions
paragraphs.text: Most of what is known about how shields erupt comes from studies of the volcanoes of Hawaiʻi Island. The island gives its name to the slow-moving eruptions typical of shield volcanoes, known as Hawaiian eruptions, which are the least explosive of volcanic events. They often happen at fissure vents. They begin with large "curtains of fire", which quickly die down and gather at particular places on the volcano's rift zones. Eruptions from a central vent often take the form of large lava fountains, which can be hundreds of metres high or more. Hawaiian eruptions often last an extremely long time: Puʻu ʻŌʻō, a cinder cone on Kīlauea, erupted without a break from January 3, 1983, until April 2018.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of lava flow
paragraphs.text: Lava flows from Hawaiian eruptions fall into two types. Pāhoehoe lava is relatively smooth and flows with a ropey texture. ʻAʻā flows are denser, blockier and more viscous, and so move more slowly. In an ʻaʻā flow, the partly hardened front steepens under the mass of lava behind it until it breaks off, and then the mass behind moves forward. The top of the flow cools quickly, but the molten underside is buffered by the hardening rock above it, so ʻaʻā flows can keep moving for long periods of time.

paragraphs.heading: How big they get
paragraphs.text: Active shield volcanoes erupt almost continuously over extremely long periods of time, and the structures they gradually build can reach extremely large dimensions. The summit of Mauna Loa lies 4,169 m above sea level, the volcano is over 100 km wide at its base, and it is estimated to contain about 80,000 km³ of basalt. Its mass is so great that the crust beneath it has slumped a further 8 km. Counting this sinking and the volcano's height above the sea floor, Mauna Loa's "true" height is about 17,170 m. Mount Everest, by comparison, is 8,848 m high.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: Shield volcanoes turn up wherever fluid lava that is low in silica reaches the surface of a rocky planet. They are most characteristic of two settings: ocean island volcanism associated with hot spots, and continental rift volcanism. Giant shield volcanoes exist on other planets of the Solar System too, including Olympus Mons on Mars and, on Venus, Sapas Mons.
